messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Fifty-year-old Arthur Vance, of European descent, had been thirty-two when the night shifted irrevocably. He had stayed late at his private psychology practice to review intake files, and on his way to the adjacent parking garage, a figure stepped from the shadows. The assault was brutal and brief, marked by the sharp, sour tang of whiskey on the attacker’s breath and the relentless, climbing wail of police sirens that drew a crowd but offered no intervention. When it ended, Arthur was left gasping on the concrete, certain that the steady clinician and devoted husband he had been was gone. In the months that followed, these specific sensory reminders began to dictate his reality. When the faint scent of fermented hops drifted from a client’s coffee cup in his reception area, or when a drill siren echoed past his office window, a visceral tightening would seize his chest, and that physical dread would quickly curdle into a profound sense of loss. Because those triggers flooded his system with panic, he had come to believe he was no longer capable of doing the things that defined him, and the sheer weight of those triggered appraisals left him feeling dead inside, hollowed out by a grief he could not articulate. From this hollowed place, his mind began to protect itself with brutal efficiency. The very thought of who he was becoming made him instinctively reach for mental barriers. Because he felt so fundamentally broken, he found himself pushing the memory away before he could fully recall it, deliberately diverting his attention the moment the assault threatened to surface. Yet the trauma refused to stay buried. The fragments that slipped through were entirely nonverbal; he couldn't seem to put the frightening event into words, leaving only a raw, wordless panic to linger in his periphery. This relentless, wordless intrusiveness only confirmed his worst fears about his own shattered state, driving him to view his body as merely an object, not like a person, something that had been used and discarded. When no visual scene appeared, he would sometimes feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, a sudden wave of suffocating terror that bypassed his cognitive defenses entirely. The cycle tightened as his internal narrative began to dictate his environment. His dehumanizing belief that he was no longer a person actively amplified his hypersensitivity to them, turning ordinary clinic noises into credible threats. He would scan the clinic’s hallway for the slightest whiff of alcohol or listen for the familiar wail of sirens, not merely because they reminded him of the attack, but because his own appraisals transformed a chronic feeling of discomfort into a self-fulfilling alarm. That chronic sense of unease forced him to isolate himself further from the very work and marriage that once sustained him, his sessions growing shorter and his notes sparse until the distance between him and his wife widened into a silent chasm. It was the collapse of his practice that finally drove Arthur back to a therapist’s office. He could no longer sit across from new patients without his hands shaking, and the emotional numbness had spread to his home life, leaving his marriage stranded in a quiet, unbreachable routine. He came seeking a way to reclaim the clinician he used to be, hoping to find a path through the numbness before he completely lost himself. What he feared most was that the hollowed man he had become was permanent, that the safety he once preached to others had been a lie, and that the night in the garage would remain the defining chapter of his life. He stayed in the room because he was tired of fighting a war inside his own head, and because, for the first time in years, he allowed himself to wonder if the pieces could be reassembled.
